A forum with USINDOPACOM partners to discuss common standards and regulations (including cyber) could replicate NATO’s standardized agreement process to improve interoperability, including the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue countries of Australia, India, and Japan, plus other key regional partners (e.g., South Korea). In addition, DOW staff might require specialized training to understand the advanced energy assets incorporated into the region’s varied energy infrastructure and how these assets can interfere with sensors. This added complexity could further stretch existing capabilities, exacerbating the risks of operational inefficiency. Global market forces will also create a more muddied operating theater. Deep-sea mining in USINDOPACOM, partly driven by increased demand for critical materials needed in advanced energy technologies, could give Chinese ships another reason to operate in contested waters. For example, in February 2025, China and the Cook Islands signed an agreement to collaborate on research and the potential extraction of critical minerals from the Cook Islands’ seabed. This agreement highlights China’s continued focus on the South Pacific while also offering Pacific Island nations more opportunities for international partnerships. Advances in deep-sea mining are significant, as they could help establish important precedents in terms of norms and legal frameworks for undersea commercial activities. These developments also have military implications, particularly concerning the potential “dual use” nature of certain seabed exploration activities. Deep-sea mining can be leveraged as both a tool and a result of foreign policy, thereby carrying broader implications for national security (Baruah 2025). C.4 Mitigations of Particular Importance to USINDOPACOM The operational and logistical challenges associated with both legacy and advanced energy technologies underscore the strategic importance of maturing and deploying emerging solutions that are not yet operational but are uniquely suited to overcoming the region’s geographic and logistical energy challenges. For example, DOW’s heavy reliance on liquid petroleum-based fuels transported by vulnerable (mostly commercial) ships (Carmel 2023) could be mitigated by adopting advanced energy technologies, such as geothermal, marine and hydrokinetic energy, hydrogen fuel cells, or even power beaming. In particular, tidal and wave energy could become a point-of-need generation alternative to expensive diesel generation for islands (Schuler and Dupont 2025), offering a resilient and locally sourced solution for remote or distributed locations. Local energy vulnerabilities in USINDOPACOM add urgency to developing point-of- need energy generation. Research and development efforts in this vein, such as the National Laboratory of the Rockies’ Distributed Flexible Fuel Production trailer, which produces natural gas from carbon dioxide, hydrogen, and methane-producing organisms at forward operating bases (Harrison and Dowe 2025), could provide solutions if continued and operationally tested. 65 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. At 16 feet long and 100 cubic feet, the trailer and control room that house this capability are compact enough to fit in the back of a C-130J, demonstrating the promise of mobile and low- footprint energy production capabilities.
